evidence.claim: Erdogan repeated that interest rates would be lowered further and that inflation would fall as a result, even as Turkey was in a currency crisis and inflation was nearing a 20-year high.
evidence.title: Erdogan says interest rates will be lowered and inflation will fall too
evidence.excerpt: Erdogan repeated that interest rates would be lowered further and that inflation would fall as a result, even as Turkey was in a currency crisis and inflation was nearing a 20-year high.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters wire reporting with a direct ruler quote and contemporaneous market context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler attribution because the claim is Erdogan's own public economic guidance.
contrary_evidence: The article itself notes inflation was near a 20-year high, and mainstream economic analysis contradicted the claim.

evidence.claim: Erdogan vowed that the central bank would continue to cut policy rates every month as long as he remained in power.
evidence.title: Turkey's Erdogan says he will keep cutting rates "as long as I am in power"
evidence.excerpt: Erdogan vowed that the central bank would continue to cut policy rates every month as long as he remained in power.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters wire with a direct ruler quote and clear temporal fit.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler attribution because it is Erdogan's own commitment about economic policy.
contrary_evidence: The article also notes that inflation had surged and the lira had slumped after earlier cuts.

evidence.claim: State advertising revenue was funneled largely to pro-government publications, while government-appointed regulators penalized independent and opposition outlets; criticizing the president and alleging official corruption could trigger penalties.
evidence.title: Special Report-Insiders reveal how Erdogan tamed Turkey's newsrooms
evidence.excerpt: State advertising revenue was funneled largely to pro-government publications, while government-appointed regulators penalized independent and opposition outlets; criticizing the president and alleging official corruption could trigger penalties.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters describes a specific financial and regulatory mechanism, with a reporter's data review and direct implications for truthful reporting.
evidence.period_fit: Published in 2022 and describing the media system active during the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Erdogan because the media-affecting bodies are part of the state architecture built and supervised under his rule.
contrary_evidence: BIK said it was not concerned with publications' views or ideology, and later the Constitutional Court said BIK violated press-freedom rights.

evidence.claim: BIK, the official advertising body, was run by a figure appointed by Erdogan in April, and RTUK's leadership was appointed by the AKP and its allies, showing that the censorship-adjacent regulatory stack was staffed by loyalists.
evidence.title: Special Report-Insiders reveal how Erdogan tamed Turkey's newsrooms
evidence.excerpt: BIK, the official advertising body, was run by a figure appointed by Erdogan in April, and RTUK's leadership was appointed by the AKP and its allies, showing that the censorship-adjacent regulatory stack was staffed by loyalists.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters names the appointees and ties them to the governing coalition, making the appointment pattern concrete.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Erdogan because these are state appointments inside the media-control apparatus under his presidency.
contrary_evidence: Reuters notes a later court ruling that constrained BIK, so the control was not entirely unchecked.

evidence.claim: A Turkish court ordered the pre-trial arrest of journalist Sinan Aygul under the new disinformation law, the first such detention under the statute, after he reported alleged abuse involving police and soldiers.
evidence.title: In a first, Turkish court arrests journalist under 'disinformation' law
evidence.excerpt: A Turkish court ordered the pre-trial arrest of journalist Sinan Aygul under the new disinformation law, the first such detention under the statute, after he reported alleged abuse involving police and soldiers.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters gives a contemporaneous account of the first use of the law against a journalist and the underlying subject matter.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Erdogan's governing party because the law was passed by its parliamentary majority and the arrest used the resulting criminal framework.
contrary_evidence: Aygul later retracted and apologized, and the government said the law was meant to protect the public from disinformation.

evidence.claim: Erdogan picked Nureddin Nebati to oversee and articulate the low-rate economic policy, and Reuters described him as having little direct economic training and as close to Erdogan's son-in-law Berat Albayrak.
evidence.title: Turkey's new finance minister in the eye of a storm
evidence.excerpt: Erdogan picked Nureddin Nebati to oversee and articulate the low-rate economic policy, and Reuters described him as having little direct economic training and as close to Erdogan's son-in-law Berat Albayrak.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a cabinet appointment with a clear loyalty and competence angle.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and relevant to the ruler-period economic team.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong attribution to Erdogan because the appointment was his and it fit the broader inner-circle economic lineup.
contrary_evidence: An AKP official in the same story said Nebati worked closely with the president and had stemmed the lira collapse.

Direct forensic or documentary proof of Erdoğan's own assets, beneficial ownership, or personal enrichment in 2022 is still missing.
Independent corroboration beyond Reuters-style reporting is still thin for the media-control and family-access claims.
Audit-grade verification of project delivery and personnel effects is still thin; the package leans heavily on official program documents and self-reported completion counts.
